title: From quantum signals to singular values
question: How did single-qubit signal processing grow into a framework for quantum algorithms—and what changes when more than one variable enters the story?

scope.summary: A selected route through QSP, qubitization, QSVT, and two generalization branches. Eight works illustrate evidence-linked research history; this is not a complete review.
scope.coverage: Eight primary arXiv records and pinned-version abstracts checked on 2026-10-16. All eight results and six semantic relationships remain proposed. No independent expert review has taken place.
scope.search_strategy: Started from the eight works in the supplied prototype. Rechecked each primary arXiv record, its version history, and abstract. This release does not report systematic database retrieval or recall.
exclusions: Applications not needed for this selected reading route.
A comprehensive history of Hamiltonian simulation and polynomial synthesis.
Claims of priority, optimality across cost models, or the current complete frontier.
gaps: Abstract-level evidence does not independently verify mathematical proofs.
Earlier prerequisites, alternative constructions, and intervening results are omitted.

results.label: Quantum signal processing
results.summary: Single-qubit rotations become a tool for Hamiltonian simulation. This is the starting point of the selected reading route.

settings.assumptions: Sparsity and access conditions of the cited work
settings.cost: Oracle queries; no end-to-end cost comparison

results.label: Qubitization
results.summary: Embedding a Hamiltonian in an invariant two-dimensional subspace provides another key ingredient for operator transformations.

settings.input: A unitary oracle and a state-preparation oracle
settings.assumptions: Hamiltonian is a projection of the supplied unitary

results.label: Singular value transformation
results.summary: Polynomial transformations extend to the singular values of a unitary subblock, bringing several quantum algorithms into one framework.

settings.input: A linear operator embedded in a unitary

results.label: A unified reading guide
results.summary: A pedagogical path connects signal processing, eigenvalue transformations, and QSVT with familiar quantum algorithms.

settings.assumptions: Pedagogical overview; not a new priority claim

results.label: Multivariable QSP
results.summary: Multiple signal oracles introduce a new branch. Its proposed characterizations must be read alongside later critiques.

settings.assumptions: Some characterizations depend on a stated conjecture

results.label: Revisiting the conditions
results.summary: A targeted critique questions Theorem 2.3 and its assumptions. This is not a rejection of the entire research direction.

results.label: QSP on U(N)
results.summary: A larger auxiliary space enables a framework for simultaneous polynomial transformations of a block-encoded input.

settings.input: A block-encoded input and U(N) auxiliary space
settings.assumptions: Distinct from arbitrary access to multiple oracles

results.label: Constructive M-QSP
results.summary: A classical decision algorithm addresses realizability for specified multivariable Laurent-polynomial pairs, with a constructive output.

settings.input: A pair of multivariable Laurent polynomials
settings.assumptions: The paper's M-QSP representation and operator model
settings.cost: Polynomial in variables and signal operators

evidence.summary: The abstract describes eigenvalue transduction, a rotation sequence, and ancilla projection for Hamiltonian simulation.
The abstract constructs an invariant SU(2) subspace using controlled access to the specified oracles.
The authors describe a generalization of Low–Chuang Hamiltonian simulation and applications to quantum matrix operations.
The tutorial explicitly builds its explanation around the Gilyén–Su–Low–Wiebe QSVT framework.
The authors introduce multivariable signal processing and discuss conditional characterizations of achievable transformations.
The comment reports inconsistencies and revised necessary conditions; it also argues those conditions are not sufficient.
The authors generalize U(2)-based frameworks to U(N) and characterize achievable polynomial matrices.
The abstract states a necessary-and-sufficient decision test and a method to construct the required signal-processing parameters.

relations.summary: The QSVT abstract explicitly generalizes Low–Chuang Hamiltonian simulation. The precise theorem correspondence awaits full-text review.
The tutorial identifies QSVT and its original authors as its central teaching framework.
The abstract proposes a multivariable counterpart to QSP; achievable transformations still have conditions.
This comment targets Theorem 2.3 and Conjecture 2.1 of the M-QSP work, not every result in the field.
The U(N) work explicitly generalizes the U(2) frameworks; detailed technical matching is not yet reviewed.
The later work addresses an M-QSP realizability problem. This connection denotes problem continuity, not a certified proof dependency.

narrative.overview: A way to shape quantum signals became a common language for quantum algorithms. Follow the move from a single signal to singular values, then see why adding more variables makes the conditions matter again.

turning_points.title: Shape a quantum signal
turning_points.summary: QSP and qubitization connect controlled polynomial transformations with the design of quantum algorithms.

turning_points.title: A common language emerges
turning_points.summary: Singular value transformation organizes a wider family of algorithms around a shared construction.

turning_points.title: More variables, new conditions
turning_points.summary: Multivariable proposals and subsequent discussion make the assumptions part of the story, rather than an invisible footnote.
